raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Central Police University broke the Constitution by refusing to admit color-blind applicants to its 2002 master's programs. The court decided the rule did not violate the constitutional guarantees of equality and equal educational opportunity. It found the rule serves an important public purpose and is substantially connected to it.
raw.held: The admission rules that decide eligibility by whether an applicant is color-blind do not conflict with Articles 7 and 159 of the Constitution.

points.text: The admissions notice is a general rule the university issued, so it counts as an 'order' the court can review.

Universities have autonomy over admission requirements, and the police university keeps a degree of it, so setting a physical-exam condition did not exceed that autonomy or breach the legal-reservation principle. It must still respect basic rights.

The right to education beyond compulsory schooling protects against arbitrary limits on students already enrolled; it does not give a right to be admitted. Excluding applicants who don't meet requirements is a problem only if it breaches equality and equal educational opportunity.

Because color-blindness is a physical condition beyond a person's control and education matters greatly, the court applied stricter review. The purpose must be an important public interest, and the means must be substantially connected to it.
The purpose is to train police professionals and use limited educational resources well, which improves policing and the rule of law. That is an important public interest.

Police work is broad, staff are often rotated, and judging colors may be needed at any time, so color-blind people have a proper reason to be seen as unsuited. The rule is therefore substantially connected to its purpose, even though graduates must still pass a separate exam and are not required to become police.

who: Color-blind applicants to the Central Police University
Other applicants and students at the police university

raw.answer: The case asked whether parts of a 2006 law creating a special committee to investigate the 2004 shooting of the presidential and vice-presidential candidates (the 319 shooting) were unconstitutional. The court found most of the challenged provisions consistent with the Constitution and its earlier Interpretation No. 585. It struck down the committee's power to fine people directly, the related fine-procedure rule, and the rule that agencies could not refuse to lend staff.
raw.held: Most challenged provisions are not inconsistent with the Constitution or Interpretation No. 585. The committee's own power to impose fines (Art. 8-2 para. 3), Art. 8-2 para. 4, and Art. 11 para. 3 (agencies may not refuse to lend staff) lose effect from the day of the ruling. The request for a provisional order needs no further review, and the challenge to the other articles was not accepted.

points.text: The Legislative Yuan's investigative power is an auxiliary power. In special cases it may appoint outside people to help by passing a detailed special law, so the committee's setup was tested against Interpretation No. 585 and the principles of separation of powers, proportionality, clarity and due process.

The committee's ability to act and sue in its own name, to hire advisers, and to borrow agency staff (with consent) fits its special temporary role. But forcing agencies to lend staff against their will breaks separation of powers and checks and balances.

The Legislative Yuan supervises the committee members and may remove unfit ones by a vote. This standard is clear enough and can be reviewed by courts. The committee's costs may come from the second reserve fund where budget rules allow.

The investigative methods in Articles 8 and 8-1 (summoning people, requesting documents, inspections, sealing or taking materials) are effective tools. They are not forced searches or seizures, and they carry protections, including consent of the court or agency concerned and court review for government agencies refusing on grounds of major national interest.

Only the Legislative Yuan, by a plenary decision, may fine those who refuse to help, so the committee's own power to fine conflicts with Interpretation No. 585. The committee may still report and publish violations. Refusals can be challenged in an administrative court, and no fine may be imposed until that case is final.
Asking police or other agencies for help is allowed because the committee merely requests it and the agencies agree to it. It does not direct them, so there is no separation-of-powers problem.

who: The special investigation committee and its members

raw.answer: The case asked whether two Council of Labor Affairs circulars were unconstitutional because they added a condition for death benefits under labor insurance: the worker's illness or injury had to arise while the insurance was in force. The court held that the circulars add a restriction the Labor Insurance Act does not contain, which breaches the constitutional principle that restrictions on rights need a legal basis. To that extent they may no longer be applied.
raw.held: The two circulars (of 1988 and 1990), as applied to death benefits, are contrary to the legal reservation principle in Article 23 of the Constitution. They may no longer be applied to the extent that they require the illness or injury to have arisen during the insurance period.

points.text: Labor insurance is a social insurance system serving constitutional policy goals. Workers' right to join it, and the public-law rights that flow from it, are protected by the Constitution.

Labor insurance is compulsory and premiums are based on ability to pay, so it differs from commercial insurance. The legislature may decide which insured events are covered, but rules on rights and restrictions must be set by law or by an order clearly authorized by law, and must meet Article 23.

Article 19(1) of the Act sets no limit on when the cause of the insured event arose. For death benefits, the insured event is the death of the insured person or of a parent, spouse or child, and when the cause of death arose does not matter.
Death benefits exist to spare a worker's family or dependents financial hardship when the worker dies, which fits the constitutional protection of workers.

Concerns such as an insured person already being unable to work when enrolling, or obtaining benefits by fraud, are handled by other means: cancelling insured status, fines, and civil or criminal liability.

The circulars required the illness or injury to arise within the insurance period, or no specified prior disease before enrolling. This adds a restriction the Act lacks, which violates the legal reservation principle. Which diseases and time links may be excluded is for the legislature to decide.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1997 rule on how much stock company directors and supervisors of publicly listed companies must hold was constitutional, specifically its provisions on who gets fined. The court found that parts of Article 8 of that rule punish all directors or supervisors together, and punish a corporate representative, without a legal basis or clear legal authorization. It held this conflicts with the constitutional principle that restrictions on rights need a legal basis, and the parts will lose effect within six months.
raw.held: The first paragraph and the latter part of the second paragraph of Article 8 of the rule conflict with the legal reservation principle in Article 23 of the Constitution and become invalid six months after the ruling is announced.

points.text: Punishing people for breaking administrative duties limits their rights, so the offence and penalty must be set by law, or by an order with clear legal authorization.

Who is punished, and how blame is shared when several people break the same duty, also limits rights. Without law or clearly authorized regulation, an administrative order cannot set them, and the default is to punish each person by the seriousness of their conduct.
The Securities and Exchange Act Article 26(2) only authorized rules on director and supervisor shareholding ratios and their checking, not on who is punished or how shared blame is assigned.
Article 8(1) punishes all directors or supervisors together and Article 8(2) latter part punishes the corporate representative, so they go beyond what Article 26(2) authorized.
Article 178(1)(4) of the Act only sets the type of violation and the penalty; it neither sets the blame method or targets nor authorizes the agency to fill them in.

Making up the share shortfall is an administrative duty, not a penalty, so requiring it after a fine does not raise a double-punishment problem. How to assign responsibility must be set by law or clearly authorized orders.

who: Directors and supervisors of publicly listed companies
Corporate representatives elected as directors or supervisors
Legal entities elected as directors or supervisors

raw.answer: The case asked whether three Ministry of Finance circulars were unconstitutional because they treat demolition and relocation compensation paid to companies as 'other income' for income tax. The court held they were not unconstitutional. It found they fit the income tax law and do not breach the principle that taxes must rest on law, equal treatment, or property rights.
raw.held: The three Ministry of Finance circulars (of 1993, 1995 and 1998) are consistent with Articles 3 and 24(1) of the Income Tax Act. They do not violate the principle of taxation by law, the equality principle in Article 7, or the property protection in Article 15 of the Constitution.

points.text: Tax elements must be set by law, but agencies may issue necessary interpretations when applying tax laws. Such interpretations are acceptable if they follow ordinary methods of legal interpretation and the law's purpose, and they must also be consistent with tax fairness.

The income tax on businesses covers both operating and non-operating gains. Together, the Income Tax Act and its enforcement rules define how income is calculated, and exemptions are listed in Article 4, so this framework does not breach the principle of taxation by law.

Compensation a company receives for demolition of structures in land readjustment is an involuntary, non-operating gain. If anything remains after deducting related costs and losses, the company has the ability to pay tax, so taxing it is consistent with tax fairness.

The circulars interpret the Income Tax Act and its enforcement rules on non-operating gains. Because this compensation is not on the Article 4 exemption list, treating it as other income and taxing the net remainder stays within the legislative intent. It also does not violate property rights.

Treating individuals and businesses differently on this compensation does not breach equality. Their tax rates, income structures, tax bases, bookkeeping duties and depreciation differ, and individuals' compensation is not exempted beyond what the law provides. So there is no unreasonable difference in treatment.
The challenge to Article 8, item 11 of the Income Tax Act was not accepted for review because that provision was not applied in the final court judgment.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 329 of the Criminal Code is unconstitutional. That article treats a thief or snatcher who uses force or threats on the spot to protect the stolen goods, escape arrest, or destroy evidence as a robber. The court decided it is not unconstitutional.
raw.held: Article 329 stays valid: it does not go beyond the legislature's reasonable freedom to shape the law, and it does not treat like things unreasonably differently. The force or threats it covers must be enough to make resistance difficult, so punishing it like robbery does not violate the principle of proportionality in Article 23 of the Constitution.

points.text: The article uses criminal punishment to protect people's physical freedom, personal safety and property from unlawful harm, which serves the constitutional provisions the ruling names (Articles 8, 22 and 15).

The three listed reasons (protecting stolen goods, escaping arrest, destroying evidence) are those that often lead to force or threats during theft or snatching, so the legislature chose the more dangerous situations to punish like robbery.

Other property crimes are rarely so closely linked in time and place to the use of force, so limiting the rule to theft and snatching is within the legislature's reasonable discretion and is not an unreasonable difference in treatment.

In these cases taking the property and using force are closely linked in time and place. The intent can be seen as one combined intent, and the harm to the victim's property and person is the same as in robbery even though the order is reversed.
The force or threats must reach the level of making people unable to resist easily, so the article does not reach mere bluffing or brief minor physical scuffles.
Because of this, heavy robbery-level punishment is not applied to very minor conduct, so the principle of proportionality is respected.

who: People accused of theft or snatching who use force or threats on the spot
Third parties who are subjected to force or threats

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's Fair Trade Act rules punishing improper multi-level marketing, and a related regulation, violate the Constitution. The court held that the Act's ban and its criminal penalty are constitutional, but that Article 5 of the Multi-level Marketing Management Measures went beyond what the law authorized and must not be applied.
raw.held: Article 23(1) and Article 35 of the old Fair Trade Act are constitutional: they are clear enough and do not violate the protection of personal freedom and property. Article 5 of the Management Measures exceeded the delegated authority, breached the legal reservation principle, and is not to be applied.

points.text: Criminal punishment of socially harmful conduct is permitted if clearly defined by law and consistent with Article 23 of the Constitution, and vague-sounding legal terms are acceptable if their meaning can be understood and foreseen and courts can apply them.

Multi-level marketing where participants earn mainly from recruiting others, not from the reasonable market price of goods or services, is improper. It drives ever more recruiting, leaves later joiners with losses, and gives organizers big profits, harming the market and economic stability, so banning it and punishing it with up to three years' imprisonment or fines serves a legitimate purpose and is not excessive.

The terms 'mainly' and 'reasonable market price' are determined by where participants' income comes from and the price of the goods or services, so their scope is determinable. Because the company plans the scheme, its operators can foresee violations, and courts can review them, so the rule is clear enough.

The Fair Trade Commission's interpretation on 'mainly' was consistent with the Act, but its view that a company with a compliant return policy can be treated as having a 'reasonable market price' when no comparable goods exist did not match the Act's intent.
Restrictions on people's rights must be set by law, and any delegation to regulations must be specific in purpose, content and scope. Contract freedom is protected by the Constitution.

Article 5 of the Management Measures gave participants rights to cancel or end contracts at will and required the company to take back goods, refund money and buy back goods, changing Civil Code rules. This concerns rights and duties on leaving a scheme, goes beyond mere administrative management, and exceeds the delegated authority.

who: Multi-level marketing companies and their operators

raw.answer: The case asked whether a provision of the 1999 Communication Protection and Surveillance Act was unconstitutional. The provision let prosecutors issue wiretap warrants during investigations, on the request of police or on their own initiative. The court held that this did not match the constitutional protection of secret communication, because the same investigative bodies both requested and issued the warrants.
raw.held: Article 5, paragraph 2 of the 1999 Act is inconsistent with Article 12 of the Constitution, which protects secret communication. It loses effect on the date of this interpretation's announcement, or at the latest on the day the revised Article 5 of July 11, 2007 takes effect.

points.text: The court could hear the case because the final judgment against the petitioner relied on wiretap evidence, and whether the wiretap was lawful depended on Article 5.

Article 12 protects people's freedom of secret communication from arbitrary intrusion. Any state restriction needs a legal basis, clear and specific conditions, no excess beyond what is necessary, and a reasonable and proper procedure.
Article 5, paragraph 1 gives a legal basis with conditions that are reasonably specific and clear.

Wiretapping is done without telling the person or giving them a chance to defend, lasts over time, deprives them of defence rights, and may harm innocent third parties. Its intrusion is even greater than that of search and seizure.
Because the intrusion is so severe, review in advance by an independent, objective judicial body is a necessary protection. Investigators should in principle apply to a court for the warrant.

Paragraph 2 lets prosecutors and police both request and issue warrants, with no checks between organs, so it is not a reasonable and proper procedure. The court also says whoever issues warrants must review the conditions strictly, follow the least-intrusion principle, and supervise execution.

who: People whose communications may be monitored
Innocent third parties whose communications may be caught

raw.answer: The case asked whether a gift tax rule violates the constitutional equality principle by exempting gifts between legally married spouses but not between unmarried opposite-sex partners. The court decided the rule does not violate equality, because it aims to protect the legal institution of marriage. It also noted that the legislature may give such partners appropriate legal protection if it does not harm marriage or other public interests.
raw.held: Article 20, paragraph 1, item 6 of the Estate and Gift Tax Act exempts gifts between legally married spouses from gift tax. Unmarried opposite-sex partners do not get the same treatment, and this is not contrary to the equality principle in Article 7 of the Constitution.

points.text: Equality means substantive equality, not mechanical sameness; a tax exemption with different treatment is allowed if there is a justified reason.
Because this is a tax exemption tied to public finances, the legislature has wide discretion. The rule is valid if its purpose is legitimate and the classification reasonably relates to that purpose.

The exemption's purpose is legitimate: spouses live together and share household finances, so their property is hard to separate, and the rule protects marriage. Excluding people in a relationship outside an existing marriage is not arbitrary, since that conflicts with monogamy.

Unmarried partners without spouses are very similar to married couples, which raises equality doubts. But the legislature's marriage requirements (registration, monogamy) have constitutional legitimacy, and the rule helps preserve marriage.
The legislature may, considering social and cultural change, give such partners appropriate legal protection if marriage and other public interests are not harmed.

who: People in relationships outside an existing marriage

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 14-1 of the Civil Servant Service Act is unconstitutional. The article bars former civil servants, for three years after leaving office, from serving as a director, supervisor, manager, shareholder-operator or adviser of a for-profit business directly related to their job in the five years before they left. The court decided the rule is not unconstitutional, but it urged the legislature to review it.
raw.held: Article 14-1 of the Civil Servant Service Act does not violate Article 23 of the Constitution and is not contrary to the Constitution's protection of the right to work.

points.text: The right to work includes freedom to choose an occupation, but civil servants owe the state special duties, so their constitutional rights can be limited. After they leave, the state may by law impose special duties on certain former civil servants to protect important public interests, even though this limits their choice of occupation.

The rule's purpose is legitimate. It aims to prevent former officials from using ties to their old agency for improper gain or using official information to help a business compete unfairly. It also aims to prevent officials from planning their post-office careers while in office, which could cause conflicts of interest or improper benefits, and so protects the integrity of civil servants.

The restriction is limited. It covers only certain positions for a set time, does not ban work in all related businesses or in unrelated jobs, and was foreseeable to civil servants. It is therefore not excessive, has a substantial link to its purpose, and is necessary to protect an important public interest.

The court added that the rule bans certain positions and breaking it carries up to two years in prison and a possible fine of up to NT$1 million, which greatly affects former civil servants. The legislature should review how it works in practice, balance integrity against freedom of occupation, and consider revising it.

who: For-profit businesses linked to former officials

raw.answer: Taiwan's Household Registration Act required people applying for a national ID card to be fingerprinted, with the prints kept on file, and refused the card to anyone who would not comply. Eighty-five legislators asked the court to review whether this was unconstitutional. The court held that the rule violated the constitutional protection of information privacy and failed the proportionality test, so it can no longer be applied.
raw.held: Article 8, paragraphs 2 and 3 of the Household Registration Act, which force people to be fingerprinted and have the prints stored or be refused an ID card, do not comply with Articles 22 and 23 of the Constitution and stop applying from the date of the ruling. Other ID card replacement work under the Act's other provisions may continue.

points.text: The court accepted the case because the legislators had tried and failed to amend the law, which fits the rule on legislators asking for interpretations.
Privacy is a basic right protected by Article 22. It includes control over one's personal information: whether, when, how and to whom it is disclosed.
This protection is not absolute. The state may collect necessary personal information by clear law if it meets Article 23, and it must clearly state the purpose of collection in the law.
ID cards are needed to exercise many rights and handle many procedures, so refusing a card for not giving fingerprints amounts to forcing fingerprinting.
Fingerprints are highly identifying and can unlock a person's full file, so mass compulsory collection needs a major public interest, a closely connected and less harmful method, and a clear law.

The Act states no purpose for the fingerprinting. Crime prevention is not a purpose of the Act. The stated aims (anti-forgery, preventing fraudulent claims or use, identifying lost or dead persons) are important, but the means are out of proportion.
Even for fingerprinting by law, the state must set a clear purpose, closely necessary scope, ban other uses, and protect the data. Foreign laws and opinion polls did not change the result.

who: People applying for a national ID card

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 12, paragraph 3 of the 1998 enforcement rules of the Civil Servant Retirement Act was unconstitutional. The rule governs how years of service at a public enterprise are counted when someone moves into the civil service. The court found it did not violate the legal reservation principle or the equality principle.
raw.held: The rule was not found unconstitutional: it did not breach the legal reservation principle in Article 23 of the Constitution, and it did not breach the equality principle in Article 7. The court did add that retirement rights of people moving from public enterprises are better set by statute or a clearly authorized order.

points.text: Benefit-type administrative measures that do not restrict people's liberties or rights do not necessarily violate the legal reservation principle. But important matters of public interest should in principle rest on a law or a clear statutory authorization.

The Constitution does not say whether public enterprise service counts toward civil servant retirement pay. The legislature may decide this by law, and before such a law exists the authority may issue reasonable rules, because they do not restrict liberties or rights.
The court noted that retirement rights for people moving from public enterprises involve important public-interest matters, so it is preferable to set them by law or a clearly authorized order.

Regulations issued under statutory authorization that are benefit-related must still follow constitutional principles, especially equality. Equality means substantive equality, so reasonable differences in treatment are allowed.
Public enterprise staff differ from civil servants, ex-political appointees, public school educators and military personnel in pay structure, fund contribution basis and rate, and benefit standards.

Because of these differences, the rule lets public enterprise staff choose to pay in to count their prior years or not count them. This is a reasonable difference, not arbitrary, so it does not breach equality.

who: Civil servants who formerly worked at public enterprises
Former political appointees, public school educators and military personnel who became civil servants

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule requiring companies to apply within six months to defer tax on stock dividends was unconstitutional. The rule applies when a company uses undistributed profits to increase capital and reinvest in certain key businesses. The court held the deadline is allowed: it does not go beyond the parent law and does not conflict with the Constitution.
raw.held: Article 42 of the Enforcement Rules of the Statute for Upgrading Industries requires a company to apply within six months after the capital increase is approved. The court held this is necessary to carry out the Statute's Article 16, Item 3, does not exceed that law, and does not violate Articles 15 and 23 of the Constitution.

points.text: Business freedom is protected by the Constitution. Limits on rights must be set by law and go no further than necessary. Implementing rules must fit the law's purpose and stay within its scope, judged by the law's purpose and overall structure rather than just its wording.

The law lets stock dividends from a capital increase out of undistributed profits be taxed later, to speed up company capital formation. Whether a dividend qualifies is for the authority to verify, and the Enforcement Rules were issued under the Statute's own authorization to carry out this deferral.
Most of the facts needed for an application are held by the company, so requiring it to apply on its own within a set period fits the law's purpose.

The six-month period is fairly short, but it does not narrow the content or scope of the tax deferral. Deferral affects state revenue and taxpayers' tax planning, so the period should not be too long.

The rule also lets a company apply before the deadline, give reasons and submit documents later, within another six months. This eases the time limit, given that getting the key-business approval letter is not easy and the investment must fit the timing of that business's capital increase.

Whether a dividend can be deferred seriously affects a company's finances and operations, so it falls within the company's protected property rights and business freedom. The company applied in its own name and sought remedies in its own name, so its request for interpretation was properly brought.

who: Companies that use undistributed profits to increase capital and invest in key businesses
Shareholders receiving stock dividends from such increases

raw.answer: The case asked whether rules on the first survey and registration of buildings owned in separate units (such as apartments) are unconstitutional. These rules are the Land Registration Rules and the Cadastral Survey Implementation Rules. The court held they are not unconstitutional, but said the law itself has gaps that should be fixed by clearer legislation.
raw.held: The Land Registration Rules and Cadastral Survey Implementation Rules for first survey and registration of divided-ownership buildings stay within what the Land Act authorizes and do not violate the Constitution's property protection, legal reservation or proportionality principles. The court also said the Land Act and related laws should be reviewed and improved to set out key matters clearly in statute.

points.text: Property rights are protected by the Constitution, and real estate registration gives public notice and credibility, so registered content must be accurate and true to protect owners and keep transactions safe.
In divided-ownership buildings, each owner's private part and the shared parts are physically linked and legally complex, so the scope and location of each must be clear before first registration.

The Civil Code presumptions about shared parts are substantive rules, but a registration procedure law may set more specific technical rules to make registered content accurate. The two have different functions.

The survey rule requires documents such as an allocation agreement among all builders when the building permit cannot fix rights, or transfer documents when the applicant is not the builder, so the land office has an objective basis for survey and registration.

The registration rule on shared parts gives the method for registering them and a standard for identifying them. These rules reflect the complexity of the relationships and the fact that land offices cannot judge substantive rights.
The rules stay within the Land Act's authorization, are needed for the procedure, and do not add restrictions the law lacks, so they do not conflict with the Constitution.

The Land Act and related laws lack clear provisions on matters important to people's rights, such as identifying shared parts, allocating ownership and shares, and resolving disputes, and some matters are left entirely to regulations. This is inadequate and should be improved by statute.

who: Owners of units in divided-ownership buildings
Applicants for first survey and registration

raw.answer: The case asked whether a customs inspection rule is unconstitutional because it lets importers avoid punishment for mixed-up shipments only when both shipments came from the same sender. The court decided the rule does not violate the constitutional principle of equality. Importers whose mix-up involved different senders are dealt with under the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act.
raw.held: The rule limiting combined handling without penalty to mistaken swaps between two or more shipments from the same sender, and treating swaps between different senders under the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act, does not violate the equality principle in Article 7 of the Constitution.

points.text: The Ministry of Finance was authorized to set inspection rules, and this rule falls within the authority given by the Customs Act.

Equality under the Constitution means real equality in legal standing, not rigid formal sameness, so an agency may treat cases differently in tax and economic matters if its aim is legitimate and the classification reasonably relates to that aim.
The rule's aim is legitimate: it secures honest declarations, prevents tariff evasion, and gives clear handling standards for smoother customs clearance.

Different treatment is reasonably related to the aim: same-sender mix-ups are more likely and easier and cheaper for customs to verify, while different-sender mix-ups are very unlikely and hard to verify, and loosening the rule would create enforcement gaps.
The choice rests on long customs experience and on verification costs and technique, so it is not arbitrary and does not conflict with Article 7.
Penalties still require intent or negligence, and the rule does not remove that requirement, so an importer without fault should not be punished.

who: Foreign shippers whose goods are mixed up

raw.answer: The case asked whether two parts of Taiwan's Referendum Act break the Constitution: the Legislative Yuan's power to put a referendum proposal to voters, and the way members of the Executive Yuan's referendum review committee are appointed. The court said the Legislative Yuan's power is not unconstitutional within limits, but the appointment rule is unconstitutional because it takes away the Executive Yuan's power to choose committee members.
raw.held: Article 16(1), letting the Legislative Yuan refer major policy disputes to a referendum, does not conflict with the Constitution when it stays within the Legislative Yuan's constitutional powers and respects separation of powers. Article 35(1), under which parties nominate committee members in proportion to Legislative Yuan seats, violates separation of powers and loses effect no later than one year after the ruling is announced.

points.text: Taiwan's system is still representative democracy, and the Constitution also gives people the right of initiative and referendum, so a referendum law that helps people use these rights is not unconstitutional.

The Legislative Yuan represents the people and has a say on important national matters and policies, so letting it refer major policy disputes to a vote does not conflict with representative democracy, and it is hard to say this invades executive power or unbalances the two branches.

Lawmakers must set clear rules and a fair, objective body to review referendum proposals, but they must obey separation of powers and may not completely strip the Executive Yuan of its personnel power.

The review committee sits inside the Executive Yuan and effectively decides whether proposals qualify, with decisions issued in the Executive Yuan's name and challengeable through administrative appeals, which makes its work executive in nature.

Executive power needs authority over personnel in its own bodies, so the Executive Yuan should have the power to appoint committee members, though the Legislative Yuan may take part or check it within limits.

Under Article 35(1), parties choose members by Legislative Yuan seat share, leaving the Premier no say and only passing nominations on to the President, which completely removes the Executive Yuan's appointment power.

who: Executive Yuan and its referendum review committee
Citizens proposing or voting on referendums

raw.answer: The case asked whether an administrative fine that has become enforceable can still be collected after the person who owes it dies. The court decided that if the person left property, the fine can be enforced against that estate, but only against the estate and not the heirs' own property.
raw.held: Once a fine decision has been made and is enforceable, and the person then dies leaving property, the fine debt can be enforced under Article 15 of the Administrative Execution Act. Enforcement is limited to the estate left at death.

points.text: If the person dies before the fine is imposed, no fine should be imposed, because the person no longer exists to bear it and punishing a dead person has no real meaning.

If the person dies after the fine but before paying, the duty to pay is personal to them. Whether the estate can be reached depends on special legal provisions, and the legislature has room to choose between treating the fine as punishment and treating it as a way to uphold public order and interest.

The Administrative Execution Act and its implementing rules list fines as a public-law money duty, consistent with the authority the law gave. Collecting such money serves administrative goals, so enforcing against the estate is reasonable and necessary.

Under current law there is no legal basis for refusing to enforce, but Article 15 limits enforcement to the estate left at death. Earlier Interpretation No. 2911 is read as meaning that, absent a special rule, heirs' own property cannot be reached.

Because enforcement against the estate limits what heirs can inherit, heirs may bring or continue administrative remedies as interested parties. The ruling covers only fines, not other public-law money duties.

who: Heirs of a person who has died

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1997 rule from a Taiwan tax bureau, allowing 10% of simplified paper-review income tax filings to be spot-checked against account books and documents, was unconstitutional. The court held that it was, because it added a tax procedure burden on people that the statute did not provide for. The rule will become invalid within one year of the ruling's announcement.
raw.held: Point 7 of the Northern Region tax bureau's simplified review rules conflicts with Article 80, paragraph 3 of the Income Tax Act and violates the constitutional principle that taxes must be set by law (Article 19). It becomes invalid no later than one year after the ruling is announced, and Interpretation No. 247 is supplemented.

points.text: Article 19 of the Constitution means that tax rules, including the procedures for collecting tax, must be set by law. Agencies may not use orders to set different procedures or add burdens, unless a law clearly authorizes it.

Under the Income Tax Act, once the authority has set an industry income standard, a filing at or above that standard is accepted as filed. This is meant to simplify collection and be convenient for both sides, but it does not remove the duty to report honestly.
Collection procedures can change taxpayers' costs and the content of their tax duty, so they must be set by law. Any authorization for an agency to fill in details must be specific and clear.

Under the Act, an income filing at or above the standard is the basis for paper review. The authority therefore cannot use an order to create its own audit procedure that calls for account books and documents.

Point 7 allowed spot checks and individual audits of filings at or above the standard. This clearly did not match the statute and added a procedural burden the law does not provide, violating Article 19.

Where concealed or unreported income is found, the authorities can still investigate and impose back taxes or penalties under the laws the ruling names. If the tax authorities want spot checks of such filings, the relevant tax laws can be reviewed and amended to say so.

who: Taxpayers whose filings are at or above the industry standard
Self-employed professionals and cram school, kindergarten and daycare operators

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 15 of the Enforcement Rules of the Land Tax Act was unconstitutional. The rule let landowners be fined three times the evaded tax if they failed to report within 30 days that the reason for a special tax rate had ended. The court held the rule unconstitutional because it added a penalty target that the law itself did not set, and no law clearly authorized it.
raw.held: Article 15 of the Enforcement Rules of the Land Tax Act violates Article 23 of the Constitution and loses effect no later than one year after the ruling is announced.

points.text: Penalties for breaking administrative duties limit people's rights, so the elements and consequences must be set by law. A regulation may do so only with clear legal authorization.
Land Tax Act Article 6 reductions and Article 18 special tax rates both lower the tax, but their purposes, standards and procedures differ, so they cannot be treated as the same.

Because the penalty provision in Article 54(1)(1) concerns penalty elements, 'reduction or exemption of land value tax' is read narrowly. It covers only reductions made under the standards and procedures of the Land Tax Reduction and Exemption Rules authorized by Article 6.
The Act's authorization to make enforcement rules does not clearly say whether or how to punish failing to report the end of grounds for a special rate.

The enforcement rule extended the threefold fine to people outside the penalty law's scope, adding a penalty target through a regulation without clear authorization, contrary to the legal reservation principle.

who: Landowners who benefit from special land tax rates
Landowners who receive land value tax reductions

raw.answer: The case asked whether two income tax law provisions that add a late-filing charge of 10% of the assessed tax (at least 1,500 in amount) are unconstitutional. The court decided they are, at least where the taxpayer has already paid the tax owed. The provisions will stop having effect no later than one year after the ruling is announced.
raw.held: The provisions on late-filing charges (Income Tax Act Art. 108(1) and Art. 108-1(1)) violate the proportionality principle in Article 23 of the Constitution and the protection of property in Article 15. They lose effect at the latest one year after the ruling is announced.

points.text: The late-filing charge punishes taxpayers who miss the legal deadline to file income tax or undistributed earnings returns. It aims to get taxpayers to file so authorities can track tax sources and run a sound review system.
The charge is a fine for failing to perform a duty (a conduct penalty), and it restricts people's property rights.
Where violations can be more or less serious, the penalty must follow how serious the breach of the duty itself is.
When the taxpayer has already paid the tax owed, the provisions still add the charge at a fixed percentage of the tax and set no reasonable maximum.
This goes beyond what is necessary to punish, so it breaches proportionality and the protection of property.

who: Individual taxpayers who filed income tax returns late
Businesses that filed undistributed earnings returns late
Tax authorities that assess the charge

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1999 revision to the rules on civil servants' pay grades was unconstitutional. The revision limited how far a civil servant's earlier service as a contract (聘用) employee could raise their pay grade, capping it at the highest basic-salary grade instead of the highest seniority-pay grade. The court decided the revision did not violate the equality principle, the principle of protecting reasonable reliance, or the constitutional limits on restricting property rights.
raw.held: The 1999 revision, which caps pay-grade advancement for prior contract-employee service at the highest basic-salary grade, is consistent with the constitution's equality protection. It also respects the reliance-protection principle and does not raise a property-rights problem.

points.text: The right to hold public office protects civil servants' pay grades, but the right to a pay-grade ranking depends first on having civil-servant appointment qualifications.
Contract employees are temporary staff hired without qualifications, grades or pay ranking, and are excluded from the civil-servant pay law, so they cannot claim pay-ranking rights.

Earlier rules let contract service reach the top seniority-pay grade even though it was never assessed as strictly as regular civil-servant service, which produced an unreasonable result. Treating the service differently to keep the system sound and seniority pay fair was not arbitrary, so equality was not violated.

Reliance on the old rules can be protected where the expected benefit could reasonably be realized, such as for people who passed the exam and began training before the revision. People who registered for the exam after the revision cannot claim such protection.

The revision served an important public interest and included a transition clause with a delayed start date of January 15, 2000. Some people lacking qualifications by then were not covered, but the transition period should not be too long, so the clause was reasonable.
The rules are a favorable measure counting pre-qualification service, and are not essentially a restriction on property rights, so Article 23 is not an issue.

who: Civil servants who earlier worked as contract employees
People who passed the exam before the revision but were still in training
People who took the exam after the revision

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 2002 Supreme Administrative Court resolution was unconstitutional. It limited the spouse's surplus-property claim, which is deducted from the estate for estate tax, to property acquired after June 5, 1985. The Constitutional Court found that the resolution cut back a deduction the law allows and added a tax burden the law does not state, so it can no longer be applied.
raw.held: The Supreme Administrative Court's March 26, 2002 resolution does not fit the constitutional requirement that taxes be set by law, and it may no longer be applied. Where a surviving spouse claims a share of the surplus property, that part is deducted from the estate and not taxed, whether the property was acquired before or after June 1985.

points.text: Under Article 19 of the Constitution, tax duties and tax breaks must be set by law or by an order clearly authorized by law. A court resolution stating a legal view may not go beyond interpreting the law or add to or reduce tax duties.

The surplus-property claim recognizes each spouse's contribution to the household, child-rearing and married life. When a spouse dies and the surviving spouse makes the claim, the claimed part is not part of the estate subject to estate tax.

When a new law applies to events completed after it took effect, courts must apply it as written. They may not split its application or write their own transition rules unless the law allows gap-filling.
The article's wording covers property acquired "during the marriage" and does not split it by acquisition date. The legislators' subjective views at the time do not override the text.

The resolution did not weigh the law's constitutional aim of gender equality and protection of marriage and family. It also did not explain why earlier contributions should be valued less, or whether that fits proportionality and equality.

Counting earlier-acquired property only costs the better-placed spouse a financial benefit that may not fit the constitution's aims. A mechanism to reduce the share when equal division is unfair exists, so trust, proportionality and equality principles are not violated.

who: Surviving spouses claiming a share of surplus marital property
Married couples who wed before June 1985 and stayed under the joint property system
Heirs of a deceased spouse facing estate tax
Courts and tax authorities applying the resolution

raw.answer: The case asked whether a Ministry of Finance letter is unconstitutional. The letter says dividends an heir receives after an inheritance begins count as the heir's own income and are subject to income tax, not treated as part of the deceased's estate. The court held that the letter does not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: The 1978 Ministry of Finance letter is consistent with the estate tax and income tax laws, does not cause double taxation, and does not conflict with the Constitution's principle of taxation by law (Art. 19) or its protection of property rights (Art. 15).

points.text: Under the Constitution, a tax authority's interpretation of tax laws, within its legal powers, does not breach taxation by law or property rights if it follows ordinary methods of legal interpretation and stays within constitutional principles and the laws' intent.

Inheritance begins at death, and the estate is valued at the time of death. When unlisted company shares are valued by the company's net assets, even if those include undistributed profits, the estate tax is on the shares, not on the company's assets or profits.

Inherited property is exempt from income tax because it is subject to estate tax. Dividends an heir later receives as a shareholder are the heir's own business income under the income tax law, so that exemption does not apply to them.

The inherited shares and the later dividends are different objects of taxation, taxed under estate tax and income tax respectively, so there is no double taxation. The court therefore saw no need to decide the general question of whether double taxation is unconstitutional.

The letter was issued under the authority's legal powers to clarify whether such dividends fall under estate tax or income tax. It fits the intent of the estate tax and income tax laws, so it does not conflict with Articles 19 and 15.

who: Heirs who inherit shares in unlisted or non-OTC companies
Taxpayers receiving dividends after inheriting shares

raw.answer: The case asked whether it was unconstitutional for the Ministry of Finance to require back-payment of land value increment tax when someone who does not farm the land buys farmland in a farmer's name. The court held that the tax rule treating farmers and non-farmers differently is consistent with equality, and that the Ministry's 1993 letter is constitutional.
raw.held: The 1989 Land Tax Act Article 39-2, paragraph 1, which treats self-farming farmers and other buyers differently, meets the constitutional equality requirement. The Ministry of Finance's 1993 letter does not conflict with the clarity principle or Articles 7, 19 and 15 of the Constitution.

points.text: The Constitution requires taxes to be set by law, but the agencies may explain technical and detailed matters. An interpretation is acceptable if it follows constitutional principles, ordinary methods of legal interpretation, the law's purpose and the tax's economic meaning.
Tax breaks for a particular group, set by law for the public interest and with proper reason, are not forbidden by the equality clause (Article 7).

The exemption from land value increment tax for farmland moved to self-farming farmers aims to ensure lasting agricultural development, sensible land use and a better farm structure, and it supports the constitutional goal of backing self-farmers.
Treating self-farming farmers differently from non-farmers who acquire farmland has a proper reason and a reasonable link to that goal, so it meets the equality requirement.
If farmland is transferred to a non-farmer but registered in a farmer's name, it does not fit the exemption's purpose, so the land value increment tax is charged on the transfer.

The Ministry's letter is a clear interpretive rule within its authority and limits the exemption to transfers to self-farming farmers. It fits the legislative purpose and farm and tax policy, goes beyond no reasonable tax limit, and does not infringe property rights.

who: People who buy farmland in a farmer's name without farming it
Taxpayers owing land value increment tax

raw.answer: The case asked whether a law reserving the massage trade for visually impaired people is constitutional. The court ruled that the rule violates the constitutional guarantees of equality, the right to work, and the proportionality principle. The rule will stop having effect no later than three years after the ruling is announced.
raw.held: The rule that only visually impaired people may work in massage (Article 37(1) of the old law, now Article 46(1)) is inconsistent with Constitution Articles 7, 15 and 23. It loses effect no later than three years after the ruling is announced.

points.text: The rule gives visually impaired people a job-reservation benefit while barring everyone else from massage work, so it had to satisfy equality, the right to work and proportionality.
Protecting the work of visually impaired people is an important public interest, backed by the Constitution's commitment to helping disadvantaged groups.

Equality: as society developed, the massage market grew and the ban became an excessive restriction on sighted people. Other people with disabilities were also excluded, and the rule has not much improved the economic and social position of visually impaired people. Goal and means therefore lack a substantial connection.
Right to work: the ban is an objective restriction on career choice, which is allowed only to protect especially important public interests and only by proportionate means.

The scope of the ban is unclear, so enforcement is inconsistent and sighted people risk breaking the law in similar work. Trained and certified people could work in massage, but the ban forces them to change careers or lose their jobs. The cost to them is out of proportion to the employment benefit for visually impaired people.

The authorities should use other measures, such as training and reserved job opportunities, and manage the massage trade carefully. The three-year period allows time for careful planning and implementation.

who: People without visual impairment who want to work in massage

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Cross-Strait Relations Act is unconstitutional. The rule says mainland-area people who were allowed into Taiwan cannot serve as public servants unless they have had household registration in Taiwan for ten years. The court held that this rule is not unconstitutional.
raw.held: The court held that the ten-year household registration requirement for serving as a public servant does not violate the equality principle in Article 7 or the proportionality principle in Article 23 of the Constitution. It also declined to hear the challenge to Article 252 of the Administrative Litigation Act.

points.text: The court only reviewed the public-servant part of the provision, because only that part affected the original case; the other parts were outside the ruling.
Equality means substantive equality, so the legislature may treat people differently for reasonable cause. Such limits on rights must still meet the proportionality principle.

The Constitution's Additional Articles allow special legislation on rights and obligations between the free area and the mainland area, and the Act is that special law. Cross-strait matters involve many political, economic and social factors, so the court should respect the legislature's decision unless it has a clear and major flaw.

The purpose is reasonable and legitimate: public servants hold public power and owe loyalty to the state, and the two sides remain divided with very different systems. The rule protects Taiwan's security, people's welfare and the free and democratic constitutional order.
Treating those who registered in Taiwan less than ten years differently is reasonable, because their understanding of the free and democratic system may differ from that of other people in Taiwan.

Ten years is within what is necessary and reasonable: it allows for adapting to society and for building public trust. Case-by-case review would be hard to do accurately and would be costly. Not distinguishing between kinds of posts is not a clear and major flaw.
The request about Article 252 of the Administrative Litigation Act was not accepted, because that provision was not a law the requesting court had to apply in the original case or in this request.

raw.answer: After the Legislative Yuan kept putting off a vote on the President's nominees for the Control Yuan (the body that impeaches, censures and audits), 89 legislators asked the court whether this was unconstitutional. The court said the Control Yuan must be kept running, so the President must nominate in good time and the Legislative Yuan must vote in good time. Failing to nominate or to vote, so that the Control Yuan cannot function, is not allowed by the Constitution.
raw.held: The President must nominate successors in good time before terms end, and the Legislative Yuan must exercise its consent power in good time. If either stays passive so the Control Yuan cannot work and the constitutional system is damaged, the Constitution does not permit it.

points.text: The Control Yuan is a constitutional organ with set powers, and its head, deputy head and members are constitutionally reserved positions. Keeping it alive and working is a duty of every constitutional organ.

The Constitution's design has the President nominate and the Legislative Yuan consent, as a check and balance. So the President must nominate before terms end and the Legislative Yuan must vote in good time.
The Legislative Yuan meets its duty by actively voting, whether it approves or rejects. If it rejects, the President must keep nominating and the Legislative Yuan must keep voting.

Constitutional organs should not stop working because of personnel changes. Taiwan's constitution and laws have no mechanism to keep the Control Yuan running when successors are not chosen, so it relies on the organs holding the personnel power to do their duty faithfully.
The Legislative Yuan's procedure committee repeatedly set the nominations aside, and the Legislative Yuan had still not voted by the date of the ruling.

The legislature may also make a law with a suitable mechanism to keep the Control Yuan running. The part of the request about disputes between the Legislative Yuan and the Control Yuan was not accepted.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Ministry of Finance letters were unconstitutional for refusing land value tax refunds when a land survey found a parcel overlapped a neighbor's and its area shrank. The court held that in such cases the tax paid on the overstated area counts as tax overpaid through a calculation error, so a refund can be available. It said the parts of the two letters that said otherwise no longer apply.
raw.held: The parts of the 1979 and 1980 Ministry of Finance letters that denied refunds under Article 28 of the Tax Collection Act, where a re-survey found boundary overlap and a smaller area, no longer apply from the date of the ruling. Refunds under that article reach back at most five years of land value tax already paid.

points.text: Land value tax is based on the total land value and area an owner holds in the same city or county, and it is progressive, so more area and value means a heavier burden.
Because the tax is progressive and based on area, it must rest on the correct land area to fit the fair-taxation principle based on real substance.
After a legal re-survey, the area recorded in the registration change governs, unless the survey result is rejected or the survey work is confirmed to be flawed.

If a re-survey finds boundary overlap and a smaller area, the earlier recorded land value total was wrong, so extra tax paid counts as tax overpaid through a calculation error under Article 28 of the Tax Collection Act.
The two Ministry letters denied refunds for changes in area, so on this point they conflict with the ruling and stop being applied.
The ruling applies only to land value tax collection, not to other taxes.

who: Land owners whose re-surveyed area shrank due to boundary overlap

raw.answer: The case asked whether a 1996 rule implementing the Civil Service Appointment Act was unconstitutional. The rule explains that 'positions at Senior Appointment grade 7 or below' means positions whose rank classification tops out at grade 7. The court held the rule is a reasonable interpretation of the law and does not violate the Constitution.
raw.held: The 1996 implementing rule, Article 15, paragraph 2, is a supplementary interpretation within the reasonable scope of the parent law. It does not violate Article 18 (right to hold public office) or Article 23 (legal reservation principle) of the Constitution.

points.text: The right to hold public office under Article 18 includes the right to advancement after taking office. Important elements of advancement must be set by law. An agency acting under statutory authorization may give supplementary interpretations without breaching the legal reservation principle, if it follows ordinary interpretive methods and stays within constitutional principles and the law's purpose.

The Appointment Act created a performance-based route to promotion alongside the exam route. The legislature limited the posts that those promoted this way could hold, to balance the weight of exam-based promotion. This was within its freedom to shape the law.

The statute's wording 'positions at Senior Appointment grade 7 or below' is unclear. It could mean they can hold at most a grade 7 post, or only posts whose rank classification tops out at grade 7 or lower. So interpretation was needed.

The implementing rule adopts the second reading. This prevents people promoted by performance from holding posts ranked above grade 7, which would make a post's cross-grade classification meaningless. So it stays within the parent law's reasonable interpretation and does not conflict with it.

who: Civil servants promoted by performance review

raw.answer: The case asked whether Taiwan's road traffic law violates the constitution by allowing repeated tickets and fines for a car that stays illegally parked. The court held that repeated ticketing does not punish the same act twice, and that the rule on ticketing every two hours does not go beyond what is necessary. It added that the law should itself spell out the authority to set the ticketing interval.
raw.held: Allowing continuous ticketing and multiple fines for ongoing illegal parking does not conflict with the principle against punishing one act twice. The two-hour interval in the regulations is not excessive, though the court said the purpose and scope of the delegation should preferably be set clearly in the law.

points.text: An illegally parked car keeps violating the rule while it stays, so each ticket counts as a separate violation and several fines are not a double punishment for one act.

Continuous ticketing with repeated fines can deter ongoing violations and is useful and necessary for traffic order and safety, but it must still meet proportionality and clear-delegation requirements.

The law gives no general standard for how continuous ticketing should be done, but the 'every two hours' rule in the regulations limits the number of fines and total cost, and so is not beyond what is necessary.
The court said the delegation of continuous ticketing power is better set out clearly in the law itself.
Letting officers tow a car after ticketing is a matter the legislature reasonably left to officers' discretion, so it does not show that continuous ticketing breaches proportionality.
The later law fixes a two-hour interval, but the court noted that authorities should be allowed to shorten it for busy roads or rush hours.

who: Traffic authorities that set the rules

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 235 of the Criminal Code, which punishes spreading and making obscene materials, violates the Constitution. The court held that it does not, because it is read narrowly under this ruling. The court said the article limits free speech and publication only reasonably, and that its term "obscene" is clear enough.
raw.held: Article 235, paragraphs 1 to 3, as narrowed by this interpretation, does not violate the constitutional protection of speech and publication, the proportionality principle, or the clarity principle. A separate part of the petition was not accepted for review.

points.text: Sexual speech and information are protected by the freedom of speech and publication, whether or not they are for profit. That protection is not absolute, and the law may limit it within the Constitution's Article 23.

Courts should generally respect the legislature's judgment about the sexual values most of society shares. But minority sexual cultures' expression must still be protected, except where restriction is necessary to protect the majority's shared sexual order.
Obscene material that offends ordinary people and harms the social order gives the legislature a legitimate aim, and punishing it is a reasonable means.

The article is read narrowly. It covers material with violence, sexual abuse or bestiality and no artistic, medical or educational value, and other obscene material spread without suitable protective separation measures. Making or holding such material is covered only when intended for such spreading. Confiscation is limited to material that breaks the first two paragraphs.
So read, the article does not over-block or discriminate against sexual speech. The limit on speech is reasonable and consistent with the proportionality principle.

"Obscene" is an open-ended evaluative term, but its meaning is not hard to understand, can be foreseen by those bound by it, and can be checked by courts. It therefore does not violate the clarity principle.

who: People who share or sell sexual material

raw.answer: The case asked whether a rule in the Ministry of the Interior's regulations on staff of industry and commerce groups was unconstitutional. The rule sets lump-sum retirement pay for staff of business associations: two months' pay per year of service, capped at 60 months and claimable once. The court held that the rule is constitutional, while saying the matter would be better set out expressly in a statute.
raw.held: Article 45, paragraph 2 of the regulations is not unconstitutional: it stays within the authorization in Article 72 of the Business Associations Act and does not restrict property rights and freedom of contract excessively. The court also said the authorities should promptly review and revise the arrangement so that it is written in law. A separate part of the petition, about Article 174-1 of the Administrative Procedure Act, was not accepted.

points.text: Restrictions on property rights and freedom of contract must be set by law and must be proportionate. When a law gives general authority to issue regulations, whether that authority is clear and whether the regulation exceeds it is judged from the law's purpose and overall provisions, not just its wording.

Article 72 of the Business Associations Act, added in 1982, gave the Ministry of the Interior a legal basis for the management regulations. Before that, the retirement pay rules were an administrative order issued under the ministry's own authority.
Business associations serve a strongly public-interest role, and their staff are important to carrying out that role. So the purpose of the authorization in Article 72 is legitimate.

Article 72 does not expressly mention retirement pay. But retirement pay relates to both staff management and the associations' finances, and the legislature added Article 72 to protect staff retirement rights, so retirement pay falls within the authorization.

The retirement pay rule does limit associations' property rights and freedom of contract. But its purpose is legitimate: securing staff in retirement and helping associations recruit good staff. It also takes account of each association's finances, and associations whose approved service rules set lower pay are reviewed with their finances in mind, so the limit is not excessive.
Because management and finances of association staff affect important rights and obligations, it is better for a law to state them expressly, and the authorities should promptly review and revise.

The petitioner's challenge to Article 174-1 of the Administrative Procedure Act only disputed how the courts applied the law in the final judgment. It did not show that article was unconstitutional, so that part was not accepted.

raw.answer: The case asked whether it is unequal treatment that people wrongly jailed or harmed through military trials could not get compensation, while those wrongly held through ordinary court cases could under the Wrongful Imprisonment Compensation Act. The court decided this violated the constitutional guarantee of equality. It allowed such claims under that Act for a limited time.
raw.held: The Act's Article 1, as intended by the legislature, and the related Notes' point 2 conflict with the equality principle because they leave out military-trial wrongful imprisonment. Until the law is amended or a new one made, qualifying military cases since 1 September 1959 may claim under the Act within two years of this ruling.

points.text: The Constitution says all people are equal before the law, so people suffering equal harm to liberty or rights must be equally protected.
Ordinary criminal trials and military trials are essentially the same in nature, both being state criminal prosecution and punishment, so harm in either should be compensable.

The Act's wording could cover military cases, but the legislature's stated scope and plan limited it to ordinary courts, and a separate military law was never made, so there was no proper justification for the difference.
Military trials gave less protection than ordinary procedure, so there is even more reason to give their victims a compensation right.
The State Compensation Act route is much stricter, so military-trial victims still face a marked unequal treatment without good reason; the Notes' point 2 has the same defect.

Until the law is fixed, military cases can claim under the Act with the two-year period counted from this ruling, and the military prosecutors' offices or courts that took over handle them; overlapping compensation must be avoided.

who: People wrongly detained or harmed in military trials
Military personnel and civilians tried by military courts

raw.answer: Taiwan's legislature removed the budget for the "judicial professional allowance" paid to the Grand Justices (and the Judicial Yuan's president and vice president) in the 2005 central government budget. The Constitutional Court held that Grand Justices are constitutional judges protected by Article 81, and that cutting this part of their pay did not fit that protection.
raw.held: The Grand Justices are judges under Article 80 and are protected by Article 81 during their terms. The legislature's deletion of their professional allowance from the 2005 budget reduced their existing pay and was not consistent with Article 81; the Judicial Yuan's president and vice president are treated the same way.

points.text: The Justices did not need to recuse themselves: the ruling is about the objective constitutional order, any effect on their pay is only an indirect side effect, and recusal by all of them would paralyze constitutional review.
Grand Justices exercise core judicial power by giving final, binding rulings in individual cases, so like other judges they are constitutional judges.
Having a fixed term, sitting as a conference, or calling decisions interpretations does not stop them being judges.
Judicial independence needs protection of status, so Article 81 applies to all Grand Justices whatever their earlier job; they differ from political appointees or ordinary civil servants.
Judges' pay may be reduced only by a law for disciplinary reasons; no organ may cut it by any other reason or means, including by not passing laws.

The allowance is part of the Justices' lawful pay, relied on for over fifty years. Deleting it in the budget changed that pay structure and left the Justices exposed to yearly budget pressure, which does not fit judicial independence.

who: Judicial Yuan president and vice president

raw.answer: The case asked whether the 1988 version of Securities and Exchange Act Article 18(1), and a related rule requiring approval to run securities investment seminars, was unconstitutional. The court decided the rules do not conflict with the Constitution's protection of occupational freedom and free speech, as long as they are read narrowly. Seminars that only give general investment information, and are not meant to analyze or recommend individual securities, are outside the approval requirement.
raw.held: The approval requirement covers securities investment advisory businesses but not seminars that only give general securities information and are not aimed, directly or indirectly, at analyzing or recommending specific securities. Within that scope, the 2000 management rule's seminar provision does not conflict with the Constitution's protection of occupational freedom and free speech.

points.text: Occupational freedom and free speech are constitutionally protected, but the state may limit them by law for important public interests if the means have a substantial link to the goal.

The rule requiring approval for securities investment seminars is a subjective-condition limit on choosing an occupation, because organizers must be approved advisory businesses with set qualifications and organizational size.
The goal is to build advisory professionalism, ensure investors get faithful and professional service, and prevent disruption of the securities market, which is an important public interest.
Seminars that give investment information are protected speech, so the rules limit speech as well as occupational freedom and must meet the proportionality test.

Read in light of the purpose and free speech, the approval rule does not reach seminars that give only general information and do not aim, directly or indirectly, at analyzing or recommending individual securities.
Given the investor makeup of the market and the advisory system, requiring approval is a means that substantially helps achieve the goal, so it is proportionate and not unconstitutional.

who: People who hold securities investment seminars

raw.answer: The Executive Yuan asked the court whether parts of the National Communications Commission (NCC) Organization Act were unconstitutional. The court held that the rules for selecting NCC commissioners, which let political parties nominate most members and screen candidates, almost completely took away the Executive Yuan's power over appointments, so they are unconstitutional. It upheld the rules on appointment by the Premier and the special review procedure for earlier decisions.
raw.held: The provisions of Article 4 (paragraphs 2, 3, 4 and 6) on selecting commissioners are unconstitutional and lose effect by 31 December 2008 at the latest; NCC acts before then remain valid. Article 4's appointment-by-Premier rules (paragraphs 3 and 5) do not conflict with Article 56 of the Constitution, and Article 16's review system is within what the Constitution allows.

points.text: The Executive Yuan is the highest administrative organ and must answer for all its bodies, including the NCC, so it must keep a real say over who sits on independent agencies. The legislature may check this power but may not strip it away or take it over.
Making the NCC independent fits the constitutional protection of freedom of communication, because it helps keep out political interference.

Under the selection rules the Premier could recommend only 3 of 18 candidates, had no say in the review, and was bound to nominate and appoint whoever was approved. This nearly wiped out the Executive Yuan's appointment power and unbalanced the two branches.

Party-proportional nominations and a party-formed review committee shifted the power to the parties, which undermines public trust in the NCC's political neutrality and its purpose as an independent agency.
Article 56 of the Constitution does not reach independent agencies, so appointment of commissioners by the Premier and the commissioners' election of their chairs do not violate it.

Article 16's review procedure is a special remedy the legislature chose for a change in the system, and the legislature has wide freedom in designing petition systems, so it is not unconstitutional. A grace period was given because immediate invalidity would halt the NCC.

who: People affected by earlier communications decisions

raw.answer: The case challenged a Taiwan law that let authorities refuse to approve a new civic group because it advocated communism or splitting up the national territory. The court decided that refusing approval on that basis, by reviewing what a group says before it is set up, goes further than necessary and conflicts with freedom of association and freedom of speech. That part of the law loses effect from the date of the ruling.
raw.held: Article 2 of the Civic Organizations Act, together with the first part of Article 53 that denies permission for violating Article 2, is unconstitutional to the extent it lets authorities review the content of political speech (advocating communism or splitting the territory) and refuse to approve a group for it. That part loses effect from the date of the ruling.

points.text: The court reviewed Article 53 (first part) along with Article 2, because the two must be applied together and the lower court's decision in effect relied on both.

Freedom of association protects forming groups, and the group's continued existence, self-governance and activities. Restricting the right to set up a group is the most serious limit, so the reasons for refusal must be strictly reviewed under the proportionality principle.
The law lets non-profit groups (occupational, social and political) be refused approval for advocating communism or splitting the territory.

Advocating communism or splitting the territory is a political view, so making it a ground for refusal gives authorities power to review speech itself and directly limits free speech, which must meet proportionality.

Political parties need no prior permission and can be banned only after the Constitutional Court decides their aims or conduct endanger the nation's existence or free democratic order, whereas this law lets officials judge speech content before a group is set up.

If an approved group is later found to endanger the nation's existence or constitutional order, its permission can be revoked. Refusing at the start merely for holding such views exceeds what is necessary, so the provisions lose effect to that extent.

who: People who want to form civic groups

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 29 of the Child and Youth Sexual Transaction Prevention Act is unconstitutional. That article makes it a crime to spread, broadcast or publish messages that induce, broker, hint at or otherwise promote sexual transactions. The court held that it does not violate the Constitution's proportionality principle.
raw.held: Article 29 is not in conflict with the proportionality principle of Article 23 of the Constitution. A message falls outside it if it is not about child or youth sexual transactions and the sender has taken necessary steps so that only people aged 18 or older receive it. The court also said the competent authority should set up a rating system if technology can strictly separate audiences.

points.text: Commercial speech that is true, not misleading and aimed at lawful trade is protected, but the protection is not absolute and the legislature may limit it by clear law.

Messages promoting sexual transactions are a kind of commercial speech, but they promote illegal activity, so reasonable limits are allowed for the public interest. Other speech that describes or studies sexual transactions is not covered.
Protecting children and youth from sexual exploitation is a major public interest and a basic human right, so the law's purpose is legitimate.
